hints: Think about what the word monodentate means in terms of number, mono means one, so how many bonds can this ligand form to the metal?
Recall what any ligand must supply to form a coordinate bond to a transition metal ion.
walkthrough:
Unpack the word monodentate**
Think of dentate as tooth, like a ligand biting onto the metal. Mono means one, so a monodentate ligand can bite only once. That means it forms only one bond to the metal centre.

Describe the bond that forms**
All ligands act as Lewis bases. Picture the ligand offering one lone pair into an empty orbital on the $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ion. Both electrons in the shared bond come from the ligand, so this is a dative covalent or coordinate bond to the central metal atom or ion.

Final answer: A species that donates one lone pair of electrons
to form a dative / coordinate bond to a central metal atom / ion.

hints: Use the fact that P is linear with monodentate $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands to work out how many ligands fit around $\text{Ag}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Work out the coordination number from shape**
A linear complex has ligands at $180^{\circ}$, one on each side of the metal. That tells you coordination number is 2, so two $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands bind to one $\text{Ag}^{+}$. Add charges: $(+1) + 2 \times (-2) = -3$, giving $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$.

hints: Identify the incoming ligand from NaCN and the outgoing ligand from P, remembering Q is also a linear complex with two monodentate ligands.
walkthrough:
Build the exchange equation**
Picture $\text{CN}^{-}$ ions from NaCN replacing the two $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands on P. Since Q is also linear, it is $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}$. You need 2 $\text{CN}^{-}$ in and 2 $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ out to balance ligands and charge: $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-} + 2\text{CN}^{-} \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-} + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$.

hints: Think about why the equilibrium lies far to the right to give mostly Q, in terms of which complex holds onto $\text{Ag}^{+}$ more strongly.
walkthrough:
Link high concentration to stability**
If almost all P is converted to Q, the equilibrium lies well to the right. That happens because $\text{CN}^{-}$ binds $\text{Ag}^{+}$ more strongly than $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ does. In A Level terms, $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}$ has a larger stability constant, $K_{\text{stab}}$, so Q is the more stable complex.
Final answer: Q is more stable than P / Q has a larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ than P.

hints: Focus on what happens to the ligands, one set leaves and a new set takes its place around the same metal.
walkthrough:
Name the swap**
The metal $\text{Ag}^{+}$ stays the same, only the ligands change. $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ is pushed out and $\text{CN}^{-}$ moves in. Any swap of one ligand for another is called ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand displacement or substitution.
Final answer: Ligand exchange / displacement / substitution.

hints: Place four ligands at 90 degrees around Pt and consider the two different ways to arrange two $\text{CN}^{-}$ and two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ligands.
walkthrough:
Draw the cis isomer**
Put Pt in the centre with four positions: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. For cis, place the two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands next to each other, for example $\text{CN}$ top left and top right, and $\text{Cl}$ bottom left and bottom right. The C end of each $\text{CN}^{-}$ bonds to Pt.

Draw the trans isomer**
Keep Pt central but now place identical ligands opposite each other. For example $\text{CN}$ top left and bottom right, and $\text{Cl}$ top right and bottom left. This $180^{\circ}$ arrangement is the trans form, distinct from cis.

Final answer: One isomer with the two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands adjacent (cis, $90^{\circ}$ apart) and the two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ligands adjacent; one isomer with the two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands opposite (trans, $180^{\circ}$ apart) and the two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ligands opposite, both drawn square planar about Pt with C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ bonded to Pt.

hints: Recall the characteristic 90 degree geometry that allows cis-trans isomerism in 4-coordinate Pt(II) complexes.
walkthrough:
Assign the shape**
With coordination number 4 and two isomers possible, the arrangement cannot be tetrahedral, which shows no cis-trans isomerism. Pt(II) with this formula adopts square planar geometry, with all four ligands in one plane at $90^{\circ}$ to neighbours.

hints: Remember the name for stereoisomerism caused by different spatial positions of ligands in square planar complexes.
walkthrough:
Name the stereoisomerism**
The two structures have the same bonds but different spatial arrangement of $\text{CN}^{-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ around Pt, cis versus trans. This is cis-trans isomerism, also called geometrical isomerism.
